exercises.title: Reading · Mcq 101
exercises.prompt: What will happen if students return their books after December 18?
exercises.passage:
Read an email.

Subject: Textbook Collection Reminder

Dear Students,

If you rented textbooks this semester, please return them to the campus bookstore by December 18. Late returns will result in a small fine. Students who have lost a book should email the bookstore for instructions before the deadline.

Best, Mimi Chen

options.text: Their grades may be affected.
They will lose the right to rent again.
They must pay the full price of the book.
They will receive a fine.

exercises.explanation: D is correct because the email clearly states, “Late returns will result in a small fine.” That means students who return books after December 18 will have to pay a fee. Option A is incorrect because the message never connects late returns to students’ grades. Option B is unsupported since there’s no mention of losing rental privileges. Option C is also wrong because students won’t be charged the full price of the book, only a fine.

options.text: It has not experienced a late return before.
It allows communication before the deadline.

exercises.title: Reading · Mcq 103
exercises.prompt: What is the main purpose of this email?
exercises.passage:
Read an email.

Subject: Office Parking Update

Dear Team,

Starting Monday, the main parking lot will be reserved for visitors only. Employees should park in the lot behind Building B instead. Please update your parking passes by Friday to avoid any issues next week. Security staff will be checking passes at the gate during the first week of this change.

Kind regards,
Tom Hardwick

options.text: To request feedback on the new visitor parking policies
To inform employees about a new parking arrangement
To announce the cancellation of parking passes for the lot behind Building B
To remind staff to have their entry passes ready for security staff

exercises.explanation: B is correct because the email explains that the main lot will be “reserved for visitors only” and that employees should park behind Building B, making the purpose to inform staff of a new parking arrangement. Option A is incorrect because it doesn’t ask for feedback, only compliance. Option C is wrong—there’s no cancellation of passes. Option D is partly related, as the message mentions security checks, but that’s not the central purpose of the email.

It will be replaced with a newer model.
It will be inspected and painted.

exercises.title: Reading · Mcq 135
exercises.prompt: According to the passage, what problem made barter an inefficient system of trade?
exercises.passage:
The Evolution of Money

For most of human history, trade depended on direct exchange. A farmer might swap grain for a pot or cloth for salt. This system, known as barter, worked only when both parties wanted exactly what the other offered. The difficulty of such “double coincidence of wants” encouraged the search for a more flexible medium of exchange. Early societies adopted shells, beads, and metals whose durability and scarcity made them reliable stores of value.

The invention of coinage around 600 BCE revolutionized commerce. Stamped metal pieces provided an official guarantee of weight and purity, allowing long-distance trade to flourish. Over time, coins gave way to paper notes backed by precious metals, and later to credit systems built on trust in banks rather than gold. Each step represented a gradual move from tangible goods toward abstract promises.

Today, the rise of digital currencies marks another turning point. Cryptographic systems such as Bitcoin eliminate the need for central authorities, replacing institutional trust with mathematical verification. Supporters see this as a democratization of finance, while critics warn of volatility and environmental costs. Whether electronic or metallic, money continues to evolve as a reflection of the societies that create it.

options.text: Each trader had to want what the other person offered.
Barter required government supervision to be fair.
Farmers could not determine the quality of exchanged goods.
Early societies needed to adopt the same system of beads and shells.

exercises.explanation: A is correct because the passage states that barter worked only when both traders wanted exactly what the other offered, which made exchanges inefficient. This lack of mutual desire for goods created serious limits to trade. The statement in B about government supervision is not mentioned at all. The idea in C that farmers could not judge quality is unrelated, and D confuses the timeline since shells and beads came later as substitutes for barter.

exercises.title: Reading · Mcq 140
exercises.prompt: According to the passage, what enables soil to act as a “living factory”?
exercises.passage:
The Hidden Life of Soil

Soil appears inert, yet beneath its surface lies one of the planet’s most dynamic ecosystems. A single handful contains billions of microorganisms— bacteria, fungi, and tiny invertebrates — interacting in intricate food webs. These organisms decompose organic matter, releasing nutrients that plants need to grow. In this sense, soil functions as both a living factory and a storage system for global carbon.

Human activity, however, is reshaping this hidden ecosystem in measurable ways. For example, heavy use of nitrogen fertilizers in Europe and China can favor a few bacterial species while killing others, upsetting the natural balance of soil communities. As these microorganisms decline, carbon that was once stored underground escapes into the atmosphere, adding to greenhouse gases. Because these changes occur below the surface, scientists describe soil degradation as a “quiet crisis” that receives far less attention than deforestation or melting ice.

Some regions are now demonstrating how soil recovery can work in practice. In India, farmers who rotate rice and lentil crops are restoring nitrogen levels naturally. The lentils host bacteria that fix nitrogen in the soil, reducing the need for chemical fertilizers and improving yields in the following rice season. These efforts show that reviving soil life is not merely an environmental gesture but a practical climate strategy.

options.text: The balance of oxygen and water maintained by plant roots
The minerals that form naturally in the soil over time
The constant addition of fertilizers invented by microorganisms
The interaction of countless organisms that release nutrients

exercises.explanation: D is correct because the author explains that billions of microorganisms interact within soil to release nutrients for plant growth, turning it into a “living factory.” The other choices miss this focus. A mentions oxygen and water, which are not discussed. B talks about minerals forming naturally, but that is not part of the explanation. C is inaccurate since fertilizers are man-made, not produced by microorganisms.

exercises.title: Reading · Mcq 145
exercises.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
exercises.passage:
The Double Edge of Facial Recognition

Facial recognition technology has moved rapidly from science fiction to daily life. Airports now allow passengers to board by looking at a camera, and some stores test systems that identify returning customers. These programs promise speed and convenience, reducing the need for tickets, cards, or passwords. Governments also use them to enhance security, claiming that instant identification can help locate missing persons or prevent crime.

The city of London provides one of the most ambitious examples. Its “Live Facial Recognition” network scans crowded streets, comparing faces with police databases in real time. Supporters praise the system for identifying suspects in large events where manual monitoring would be impossible. However, independent reviews have shown that accuracy can vary depending on lighting, camera angle, and the diversity of the population being scanned. Civil rights groups have challenged the practice in court, arguing that it collects personal data without consent and risks normalizing mass surveillance.

The London case highlights the dilemma faced by many societies: efficiency versus privacy. The same algorithms that can protect the public can also track it. Whether facial recognition becomes a trusted guardian or a tool of control depends not only on its accuracy but on the values guiding its use.

options.text: Facial recognition offers both convenience and risks.
Governments should ban facial recognition because it violates civil liberties.
The success of facial recognition depends on its technological accuracy.
The London system has proven that large-scale surveillance is reliable.

exercises.explanation: A is correct because the passage explores both the advantages and dangers of facial recognition technology. The author notes its convenience and efficiency but also raises concerns about privacy and surveillance. B goes too far by calling for a ban, which the passage never suggests. C captures only one part of the issue by focusing on accuracy, and D misrepresents the author’s point since the London system is not described as completely reliable.

exercises.prompt: All of the following are mentioned as ways nostalgia can be triggered EXCEPT
exercises.passage:
The Pull of Nostalgia

The warm, sometimes bittersweet feeling that arises when recalling the past, known as nostalgia, was once viewed as a kind of illness, a longing that distracted people from the present. Today, psychologists see it differently. Rather than a symptom of homesickness, nostalgia is understood as a common and often beneficial emotion that helps maintain psychological balance during times of stress or uncertainty.

Experiments have shown that nostalgic memories activate brain regions linked to reward and comfort. In one study, volunteers who listened to popular songs from their teenage years felt more connected to others and reported higher self-esteem than those who heard unfamiliar music. A similar effect occurred when participants read old letters or viewed childhood photos: the recollections reduced feelings of loneliness and sharpened their sense of personal identity. These responses seem to work partly through storytelling—people reconstruct the past in ways that make it meaningful, reinforcing a sense of continuity between their younger and present selves.

Nostalgia, then, does more than recall what has been lost; it reaffirms what endures. By weaving past experiences into current life, individuals strengthen resilience and emotional stability.

Reading old letters

exercises.explanation: B is correct because discussing shared experiences is not listed among the ways nostalgia can be triggered. The passage specifically mentions listening to songs, reading letters, and viewing childhood photos. Hearing music, reading, and seeing images all appear in the text, while conversation does not.

exercises.title: Reading · Mcq 155

exercises.passage:
The Rise of the Telegraph

Before the nineteenth century, communication could travel only as fast as a messenger on horseback or a ship at sea. News, orders, and personal letters often took weeks or months to reach their destinations. That changed dramatically with the invention of the telegraph. Using electric signals sent through wires, people could transmit messages across vast distances in seconds, transforming both business and daily life.

The first major network was developed in the 1840s by Samuel Morse in the United States. His system converted words into patterns of short and long electrical pulses, known as Morse code. Telegraph offices soon lined railroad stations, allowing traders to track prices and newspapers to report events almost as they happened. During the American Civil War, generals used the telegraph to coordinate troop movements, demonstrating how information could become as decisive as weaponry. Similar systems spread across Europe and later under the oceans, connecting continents through submarine cables.

The telegraph compressed the world. It reshaped politics, commerce, and journalism by introducing the idea of instant communication. Though later replaced by telephones and the internet, the telegraph laid the first electronic foundation for the global networks that now link nearly every part of human society.

options.text: The spread of international communication

Improvements in transportation speed
Changes in political and commercial life

exercises.explanation: C is correct because improvements in transportation speed are not discussed as an effect of the telegraph. The passage describes faster communication, political and commercial changes, and international connections, but it never claims that transportation itself became faster.

exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in a history class. The Green Revolution refers to the period during the mid-twentieth century when dramatic increases in agricultural production transformed food systems around the world. It began with the development of high-yield crop varieties, particularly wheat and rice, combined with new irrigation methods and synthetic fertilizers. These innovations helped countries such as India and Mexico reduce famine and feed rapidly growing populations. In some regions, harvests doubled or even tripled within a decade. Yet these gains came with trade-offs. Reliance on chemical fertilizers and pesticides led to soil degradation and water pollution, while small farmers who couldn’t afford new technologies were often left behind. Agricultural diversity also declined as a few high-yield species replaced traditional crops that had been cultivated for centuries. The Green Revolution reshaped not only farming but also global economics and politics. Nations that once relied on food imports became exporters, altering trade relationships and patterns of rural migration. Today, agricultural scientists are reexamining its legacy as they search for ways to balance productivity with sustainability. Many researchers argue that a new kind of “green revolution” is needed—one that combines modern science with ecological farming practices. In upcoming discussions, we will consider how these efforts are addressing challenges like climate change, soil restoration, and equitable food distribution.

options.text: How animals survive cold temperatures through hibernation

exercises.explanation: The central idea is how water can remain liquid below its normal freezing point and why that matters. Options A and C misframe the scope. Option D elevates applications to the main idea when they are a later implication.
exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in a physics class. Under normal conditions, water freezes at zero degrees Celsius. But in some situations, it can stay liquid even when the temperature drops below that point. This unusual process is called supercooling. It happens when there is nothing in the water for ice to form around. Usually, small bits of dust or rough surfaces give the ice crystals a place to start growing. Without those, the water molecules keep moving freely, and the liquid does not turn into ice right away. In nature, this ability can be a powerful survival tool. Some insects, fish, and frogs use supercooling to survive harsh winters. The wood frog is one of the most striking examples. During cold months, most of its body actually freezes, but special substances inside its cells stop ice from forming in the organs that matter most. Its heartbeat and breathing come to a complete stop, yet when the weather warms, the frog thaws and returns to life. Scientists are interested in how these animals control freezing so precisely. If humans could copy their strategy, it might help store delicate materials like organs, blood, or vaccines for longer periods without damage. Studying supercooling reveals how living things adapt to extreme cold and how nature often solves problems that science is still trying to master.

exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in an environmental science class. We often think of sweating as an uncomfortable part of being hot, but it’s actually one of the body’s most efficient cooling systems. The process behind it, evaporation, has fascinated scientists for centuries and plays an important role far beyond human biology. When a liquid turns into vapor, it takes heat energy from its surroundings. This is why wet skin feels cooler when a breeze passes over it: energy leaves the surface as the water molecules escape into the air. Engineers and biologists have both learned from this principle. In desert climates, some plants have evolved tiny pores that open only at night to release moisture, conserving water while still controlling temperature. People have applied similar logic to design evaporative cooling systems, sometimes called “swamp coolers,” which chill indoor air using water instead of electricity-hungry refrigerators. These systems work best in dry areas, where evaporation happens quickly. Evaporation also influences global weather. As ocean water evaporates, it adds moisture to the air that later falls as rain, driving the planet’s water cycle. From our own sweat to vast atmospheric systems, the same principle connects life and climate. This simple exchange between liquid and vapor shows how an everyday process can control patterns far larger than ourselves, shaping both the weather above us and the conditions we live in.

exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in an economics class. In economics, the term opportunity cost refers to the value of what we give up when we choose one option over another. Every decision, large or small, involves a trade-off. Even when money isn’t directly involved, time, energy, or resources are still being spent in one direction instead of another. Recognizing these trade-offs helps individuals and organizations make smarter choices. Consider a student deciding whether to work part-time or focus entirely on studying. The paycheck might be appealing, but the opportunity cost is the study time and potentially higher grades that could lead to better opportunities later. Businesses face similar decisions on a larger scale. A company might invest heavily in a new product line, but doing so means giving up funds that could have been used for research, marketing, or expansion. Economists often note that overlooking these unseen costs can lead to poor decision-making. Governments also deal with opportunity costs when setting budgets. exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in a history class. More than four thousand years ago, ancient Egypt entered a period of extraordinary ambition under a ruler named Khufu. During his reign, workers began constructing a monument that would remain one of the world’s largest structures for millennia: the Great Pyramid at Giza. The pyramid was not simply a tomb. It represented a vision of order, permanence, and divine power that defined Egyptian civilization. The building process stretched over decades and required an enormous labor force. Contrary to old myths, the workers were not slaves but skilled laborers who lived in nearby villages. Teams cut limestone blocks from quarries along the Nile and transported them by boat to the construction site. Ramps made of mud and stone helped move each block into place, one layer at a time. The coordination of this effort suggests a sophisticated system of management, with overseers directing specialized crews for various tasks. The precision of the final structure remains astonishing. Even today, engineers debate how ancient builders achieved such accuracy with simple tools. To the Egyptians, the monument was not only a royal tomb but a bridge between the human and divine worlds. Next, we will explore how later pyramids reflected changing ideas about kingship and the afterlife in ancient Egypt.

exercises.title: Listening · Mcq 113
exercises.prompt: What example does the speaker use to illustrate the concept of the looking-glass self?

options.text: A musician receiving applause after a concert

exercises.explanation: The student imagining classmates’ reactions during a presentation perfectly illustrates how people build self-concept through perceived feedback. The example demonstrates how imagined judgments can shape emotion and confidence. The other options refer to different social settings that the speaker never uses to explain the theory.
exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in a sociology class. In sociology, the concept of the looking-glass self explains how a person’s sense of identity develops through social interaction. The term was introduced by the early sociologist Charles Horton Cooley, who suggested that people form their self-image based on how they believe others see them. In other words, we understand who we are by imagining the reflections of ourselves that others project back to us. This process happens in three main stages. First, a person imagines how they appear to someone else. Second, they imagine how that person evaluates them. Finally, they experience an emotion, such as pride or embarrassment, based on that imagined judgment. For example, when a student gives a class presentation, they might picture how their classmates view their performance. If they imagine approval, they may feel confident; if they imagine criticism, they may feel anxious. Over time, these repeated social reflections shape the student’s confidence, behavior, and even long-term self-concept. The looking-glass self highlights the importance of feedback in social life. Our identities are not formed in isolation but through ongoing interaction with others. In modern settings, this idea extends beyond face-to-face encounters. Social media, for instance, multiplies the number of “mirrors” people encounter each day, as likes and comments reinforce or challenge their sense of self.

exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in an art history class. The architecture of ancient Rome remains one of the most influential legacies of the classical world. Roman builders combined engineering precision with artistic ambition, producing structures that were both functional and monumental. The widespread use of concrete allowed them to create large, durable forms that earlier civilizations could not achieve. Buildings like the Colosseum and the Pantheon demonstrate this mastery. The Colosseum’s tiered seating and network of corridors reveal an understanding of crowd movement, while the Pantheon’s massive dome, supported by hidden arches, reflects an advanced grasp of weight distribution. These architectural achievements were not isolated feats but part of a broader civic vision that linked architecture to empire. Public buildings symbolized Rome’s power and order. Aqueducts carried water for baths and fountains, while forums and basilicas became centers of political life. Even distant provinces adopted Roman styles as a mark of prestige and unity. When the empire eventually declined, its architectural principles endured, shaping Renaissance cathedrals and modern government buildings. Historians and engineers continue to study how Roman techniques spread through conquest and adaptation. My next lecture will examine how these methods influenced later architectural movements and the development of urban infrastructure in Europe.

The tragedy of the commons describes a situation in which individuals, pursuing their own immediate benefit, overuse and eventually destroy a shared resource. The idea was popularized by a famous ecologist who illustrated it with a simple story about how several herders shared a common pasture. In the story, each herder gains by adding another animal, but if all the herders do so, the grass is depleted and the pasture collapses. What benefits one person in the short term harms everyone in the long run. This dynamic appears in modern contexts such as overfishing and air pollution. Each factory or fishing boat acts rationally on its own, yet collectively they exhaust the resource they depend on. Economists and policymakers have responded with various management approaches, from government regulation to community-based agreements that assign shared responsibility. In some coastal villages, for example, local fishers cooperate by limiting catch sizes, protecting their livelihood through collective restraint. The tragedy of the commons continues to shape debates about climate change and sustainable development. Researchers examining these cooperative systems aim to understand which social structures succeed in balancing individual incentives with the preservation of the common good.

Dr. Carter
Today, we will look at the evolving
landscape of higher education, particularly
how online learning platforms are
influencing traditional college experiences.
Given the current global increase in virtual
classrooms, it's essential to consider their
impact on learning outcomes and student
engagement. Do you think that online
learning will eventually replace in-person
education at universities? Explain why you
think so.

Student comments (Alice, Ben):
In my view, online learning offers a viable alternative to traditional education, especially for those who require flexibility due to work or personal commitments. The ability to access resources at any time and manage one's schedule can significantly enhance learning efficiency and accessibility. In time, I think that even more schools will offer online classes.

Though there are some benefits of online learning, I believe it lacks critical aspects of in-person experiences, such as spontaneous classroom interactions and direct peer collaboration. These elements are crucial for developing soft skills and a deeper understanding of academic material. I think that students who learn via online platforms miss out on this part of the academic experience.
exercises.sampleAnswer: “Do you think that online learning will eventually replace in-person education at universities? Explain why you think so.” Considering the evolving landscape of higher education, I see online learning as a valuable option but not a complete replacement for traditional classroom settings. I have taken several online courses while studying in Berlin, where the flexible schedule helped me manage both my studies and part-time work. However, I missed the immediate feedback and lively discussions that occur during face-to-face classes. I agree with Ben that the lack of direct interaction can hinder the development of soft skills that are often built through spontaneous group work. I think that online learning must evolve to create more engaging and interactive environments that simulate the benefits of in-person education. Enhanced virtual classrooms with real-time collaboration tools could help close this gap, making the online experience more effective for students.

Student comments (Juan, Allison):
I believe automation will benefit the workforce by enhancing efficiency and creating high-skilled jobs in sectors like AI and robotics. This shift could lead to increased job satisfaction as people engage in more creative and less monotonous work, fundamentally improving our quality n of life.

While Juan makes a valid point about job creation in certain sectors, I'm concerned about the widespread job losses among less skilled people. Not everyone can transition into high-tech roles, so automation could widen the gap between the wealthy and the poor. Therefore, I think the harms could on outweigh the benefits, especially in the short to medium term.
exercises.sampleAnswer: “Given these changes, do you believe that automation will ultimately benefit or harm workers? Explain why you think so?” In my opinion, automation will end up harming workers ten or twenty years down the road. My personal belief is that when a company has a choice between compensating an employee or utilizing cheap technology, the company will almost always choose to use technology. For example, the car manufacturing industry used to employ tens of thousands of workers, but due to advances in technology, the workforce has been reduced to a fraction of what it was fifty years ago. While Juan raised a relevant point about efficiency leading to the creation of new jobs, I believe he is missing a critical idea. To be more specific, high-skilled jobs like programming and game design are already disappearing due to the advent of AI technology that can do the same job for almost nothing.

When it comes to social media, I think the negatives outweigh the positives. Social media often promotes unrealistic expectations and can lead to issues like anxiety and depression. Moreover, it's a breeding ground for misinformation, which n can have serious societal implications.
exercises.sampleAnswer: “What do you think? Do you believe the impact of social media on society is predominantly positive or negative? Explain why you think so.” Frankly, I lean toward the view that the negative effects of social media outweigh its benefits. I agree with Ben's concerns about the platforms promoting unrealistic standards that can trigger anxiety and depression. During my first year studying abroad in Germany, I spent countless hours scrolling through Instagram, which left me feeling inadequate and drained. I vividly recall one period when the constant barrage of perfect lifestyles and curated images made me question my own achievements, ultimately affecting my sleep and self-esteem. Moreover, I encountered instances of misleading information on Facebook that spread rapidly without proper fact-checking, resulting in confusion about local events. Such experiences have taught me that while social media connects people, it can also distort reality and create unhealthy expectations.

A fully cashless society is the best way forward because it simplifies transactions and reduces crime. Digital payments are faster, more secure, and eliminate risks associated with carrying cash, such as theft or loss. Many countries, like Sweden, have ya already embraced digital payments with great success, making everyday transactions more efficient for both businesses and consumers.

Relying entirely on digital payments could create serious problems, particularly for people who lack access to banking services or who have poor digital literacy. I strongly believe that cash is still essential for those in rural areas. It is also useful for elderly populations and lower-income groups who id may not have smartphones or credit cards. Additionally, a cashless society increases dependence on technology, which could be a problem during system failures or cyberattacks.

Not handling physical cash means there is less risk of theft or loss, and transactions become more efficient during busy shopping hours. I’ve also read that countries like Sweden have embraced cashless systems, which have reduced crime and streamlined economic activities. Digital payments offer clear records that help both consumers and businesses manage their finances better. Although some worry about privacy issues or excluding those who are not tech-savvy, I believe that with proper education and secure systems, these concerns can be resolved.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 1-1
exercises.prompt: Thank you for speaking with me. Let’s begin with something simple. Have you worked on any group projects at school? What kind of tasks did your group have to complete? For example, did you have to create a presentation, do research, or give a speech?
exercises.sampleAnswer: Yes, I’ve done several group projects, but the one that stands out was in my second-year mechanical design class, which was kind of like a robotics class, basically. My team had to build a small robot that could follow a line on the ground and avoid things on the floor. I was in charge of programming the sensors, while others worked on the frame and the wiring. We spent weeks in the lab testing and fixing things that didn’t work. In the end, our robot actually won second place in a campus competition, which felt amazing. That project taught me how much communication and patience matter when people have different ideas but share the same goal.

Please answer the interviewer’s questions. #1 You have agreed to participate in a research study about teamwork. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 1-2
exercises.prompt: That sounds interesting. When you work in a group, do you prefer to take the lead or follow directions from others? Why?
exercises.sampleAnswer: Hmm, that’s a good question. I guess I usually prefer to take the lead when I work in a group. It’s not because I want control, but I like organizing things and making sure everyone knows what to do. When no one takes charge, people end up talking in circles and nothing gets done. During my robot project at university, for example, everyone had strong opinions about the design, and it started to get messy. I decided to step up and make a schedule that divided the work fairly. After that, things finally started to move forward. I don’t mind listening to different opinions, but I’ve learned that sometimes someone just has to take charge so the team can make progress.
exercises.scenario: Take an Interview Directions: On test day, you will be asked four questions and have 45 seconds to respond to each. You will not be given any time to prepare. Please answer the interviewer’s questions. #1 You have agreed to participate in a research study about teamwork. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 1-3
exercises.prompt: I see. Many universities encourage teamwork to prepare students for professional life. Do you think group projects will become even more common in education in the future? Why or why not?
exercises.sampleAnswer: Yes, I think they definitely will. In almost every job these days, you have to work with other people, so universities are trying to help students build those skills early. In my department, group work used to be limited to a few classes, but now almost every course has at least one project that requires teamwork. I think it makes sense, because technology is making work more connected. I learned in one of my classes last semester that engineers in different countries can work on the same design through shared software, so being able to communicate and cooperate is essential. Even though group projects can be frustrating sometimes, they prepare you for what real workplaces are like.

Please answer the interviewer’s questions. #1 You have agreed to participate in a research study about teamwork. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 1-4
exercises.prompt: That’s a good point. Finally, some people believe teamwork helps people develop communication skills. Do you agree with this idea, or do you feel teamwork slows down individual progress? Explain why you think so.
exercises.sampleAnswer: I completely agree that teamwork improves communication skills. When I first started university, I wasn’t very comfortable speaking in English during group discussions. I was always worried about making a mistake or sounding stupid, but working with classmates changed that. In one project, I had to explain my code to an exchange student from Germany who didn’t understand Korean, so I had to find simple words and be patient. Over time, we got to know each other and became good friends because we had the shared experience of lacking confidence in English. It’s funny, actually, that shared insecurity made it even more fun to communicate. I still like working alone sometimes, but I know that without teamwork, I wouldn’t have learned how to work through difficult times.

Please answer the interviewer’s questions. #1 You have agreed to participate in a research study about teamwork. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 2-1
exercises.prompt: Glad to have you here. Let’s start with your daily routine. When you have a busy day, how do you usually organize your schedule? For example, do you use a scheduling app on your phone, a printed calendar, or do you try to remember everything on your own?
exercises.sampleAnswer: When my day gets busy, I rely completely on my phone to stay organized. I use Google Calendar for appointments and the Notes app for my daily tasks. Between my job at the pharmacy and taking care of my kids, there’s no way I could remember everything on my own. For example, on school mornings, I check my phone right after breakfast to see what I have lined up, maybe a doctor’s appointment for my daughter or a delivery coming to the pharmacy. I also set small reminders, even for simple things like picking up groceries or calling a friend back. It makes my day feel smoother and less stressful. I think it makes sense to use technology because life just moves too fast to keep everything in your head.
exercises.scenario: #2 You have agreed to participate in a research study about how students manage their time. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 2-2
exercises.prompt: I understand. Let’s move on and discuss scheduling for the future. Do you like to make a lot of appointments and have a busy schedule, or do you prefer to limit scheduled meetings and keep your days open?
exercises.sampleAnswer: I definitely prefer to keep my days a little open. When I first moved to the U.S., I tried to plan every hour because I wanted to stay on top of everything, things like work and school, and chores, but I ended up feeling exhausted. The main reason I prefer a lighter schedule now is that I need flexibility. For example, sometimes one of my children gets sick or my husband’s work schedule changes, and I have to adjust my plans quickly. Having too many appointments makes that impossible. So I still plan the important things, like deadlines and meetings, but I also leave time to rest or just sit with my family in the evening. I’ve learned that being constantly busy doesn’t always mean being productive.
exercises.scenario: #2 You have agreed to participate in a research study about how students manage their time. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 2-3
exercises.prompt: These days, many people say they struggle to focus because of smartphones and social media. Do you think technology helps us manage time better? Or does it mostly create distractions?
exercises.sampleAnswer: I think it depends on how we use it, but for most people, it creates more distractions than it solves. I see that in my own life. The main reason is that phones mix work and personal things together, so it’s hard to separate them. For example, I might open my phone to check my pharmacy schedule, and then I notice a message from my sister in Egypt or a new post from a friend. Ten minutes later, I’m still scrolling and completely forget what I wanted to do. At the same time, I can’t deny that some apps help me stay organized. I guess technology is fine in small amounts, but too much can take away your focus and energy.
exercises.scenario: #2 You have agreed to participate in a research study about how students manage their time. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 2-4
exercises.prompt: You’ve made some good points. Finally, some people believe being busy is a sign of productivity. Do you agree with this idea, or do you think people are more productive when they have downtime? Explain why you think so.
exercises.sampleAnswer: I don’t believe being busy always means being productive. When I was younger, I used to think that if I filled every minute, I was doing well. But after moving here and starting a new life, I realized that constant activity can actually make you less effective. For example, last year I was studying for my pharmacy license while working part-time and taking care of my kids. I hardly took any breaks, and eventually I started making mistakes at work because I was exhausted. After that, I began giving myself short breaks during the day—just a walk outside or a cup of tea—and I noticed my focus improved. I think people do their best work when they have time to breathe and clear their minds.
exercises.scenario: #2 You have agreed to participate in a research study about how students manage their time. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 3-1
exercises.prompt: Thanks for joining me. Let’s start off by discussing the environment. What kinds of environmentally friendly actions do you or your family take at home? For example, do you recycle, use a bicycle, or try to conserve water at home?
exercises.sampleAnswer: At home, my family and I try to be as environmentally friendly as we can. The first thing we focus on is reducing waste. We recycle plastic, glass, and paper every week, and we try to avoid using paper plates or cups. Actually, when my parents visit from India, they always laugh because we use cloth napkins instead of paper ones. Another small thing we do is save water. I turn off the tap when I brush my teeth, and I only run the dishwasher when it’s full. It’s nothing huge, but I think it makes sense that small daily habits can add up over time. Living in Toronto also helps because the city makes recycling really easy, so it feels natural to do it.
exercises.scenario: #3 You have volunteered for a research study about people’s environmental habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 3-2
exercises.prompt: Okay, that makes sense. If you had to choose, would you rather live in a city that focuses on reducing pollution or one that invests more in public parks and green spaces? Why?
exercises.sampleAnswer: That’s a tough choice, but I’d probably choose a city that invests in green spaces. The main reason is that parks make a city feel alive and healthy. When I first moved to Toronto, I lived near High Park, and I used to go for walks there almost every evening. It wasn’t just about the nature itself but also the people, the families, the joggers, and the kids playing soccer. Green areas make people want to be outside, and that creates a cleaner, more balanced environment overall. Of course, reducing pollution is important too, but I think if a city invests in parks and trees, it naturally helps the air quality and people’s mental health at the same time.
exercises.scenario: #3 You have volunteered for a research study about people’s environmental habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 3-3
exercises.prompt: That’s a thoughtful answer. Many cities now promote bike-sharing and public transportation to cut emissions. Do you think more people will actually choose these options in the future? Why or why not?
exercises.sampleAnswer: I think more people will start using them, but change takes time. The main reason is that people need convenience. If bike-sharing stations and buses are easy to access and safe to use, then people will make the switch. For example, in Toronto, there’s a program called Bike Share, and I use it sometimes to get to work when the weather is nice. It’s cheaper than driving, and I avoid sitting in traffic. But I also notice that during winter, hardly anyone rides because it’s just too cold and slippery. So I think it depends on how well the system fits people’s daily lives. The idea makes sense, but cities have to keep improving safety and accessibility before everyone will use it regularly.
exercises.scenario: #3 You have volunteered for a research study about people’s environmental habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 3-4
exercises.prompt: Interesting. Let’s wrap up with this: some people believe that individual efforts, like recycling, make a real difference. Do you agree with this idea, or do you think that only governments can solve environmental problems? Explain your answer.
exercises.sampleAnswer: Hmm, that’s a hard question. I guess I’d say individual actions do make a difference, even if they seem small. When people start changing their habits, it creates a kind of ripple effect. For example, when I first came to Canada, I wasn’t used to sorting my trash into recycling and compost. At first, it felt like extra work, but after a few weeks, it became a habit. Now, when friends visit me from India, they automatically copy what I do because they see it’s normal here. That small change keeps spreading. I think governments play a big role in setting the rules, but if people don’t actually follow them, nothing changes. It really starts with individuals doing their part.
exercises.scenario: #3 You have volunteered for a research study about people’s environmental habits. You will have a short online interview with a researcher. The researcher will ask you some questions.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 4-1
exercises.prompt: Thank you for participating in our study. I’d like to start with a question about your study habits. When you study, do you prefer to work alone or with classmates? Why?
exercises.sampleAnswer: Hmm, that’s a good question. I used to really enjoy studying with classmates, but over time I realized I focus better when I’m alone. exercises.title: Reading · Mcq 29
exercises.prompt: The word “linger” in the passage is closest in meaning to
exercises.passage:
The Chemistry of Volcanoes

Volcanoes are often viewed simply as sources of lava and ash, but they are also powerful chemical systems that shape Earth’s atmosphere. When magma rises toward the surface, dissolved gases like water vapor, carbon dioxide, and sulfur dioxide escape, driving explosive eruptions. The balance among these gases largely determines how violent an eruption becomes.

Sulfur dioxide is of particular interest to scientists because it reacts with water vapor to form aerosols—tiny droplets that can reflect sunlight. After a major eruption, these aerosols may linger in the stratosphere for months or even years, slightly cooling Earth’s surface. For example, the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines lowered global temperatures by about half a degree Celsius for more than a year.

Not all eruptions have the same impact. Small but frequent events release gases gradually, whereas massive eruptions can inject enormous quantities into the upper atmosphere almost instantly. The height at which gases are released determines whether their influence remains local or becomes global.

Volcanic gases also interact with life at ground level. While sulfur dioxide can harm lungs and vegetation, volcanic soils enriched with minerals eventually foster fertile landscapes. This dual effect—destructive and regenerative—illustrates how volcanoes contribute both hazards and long-term ecological benefits.

options.text: remain
disappear
expand
scatter

exercises.explanation: A is correct because “linger” means to remain or stay in place for a long time. The passage says, “These aerosols may linger in the stratosphere for months or even years,” meaning they stay there. B is incorrect because “disappear” is the opposite meaning. C and D are incorrect because “expand” and “scatter” do not fit the context of staying in one location.

Charred bones and plant remains found near ancient hearths reveal that cooking was not just accidental but deliberate. Transforming raw food with heat altered its texture and flavor, making it easier to chew and digest. These changes had far-reaching effects, both biological and social.

Cooking made more calories available from the same ingredients, which may have helped fuel the growth of the human brain. Meals prepared around a shared fire also encouraged cooperation and communication. Anthropologists argue that these gatherings became centers for storytelling and teaching, giving rise to more complex social relationships. In this sense, cooking may have been as much about community as nutrition.

Today, the practice still connects people. Whether in family kitchens or public festivals, cooking expresses culture and identity. The origins of this activity remind us that a basic human need evolved into a defining social ritual, one that continues to shape how societies organize daily life and celebrate shared experiences.

options.text: It led to the decline of group interaction around fires
It replaced hunting as the main form of cooperation
It discouraged the sharing of resources
It encouraged the development of spoken language

exercises.explanation: D is correct because the passage states that cooking “encouraged cooperation and communication” and that gatherings around fires became centers for “storytelling and teaching.” These points suggest that cooking may have encouraged the development of spoken language. A is incorrect because the text says the opposite—cooking increased social interaction, not its decline. B is incorrect because hunting is never said to have been replaced by cooking. C is incorrect because cooking promoted sharing and cooperation, not the discouragement of sharing resources.

exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in a biology class. Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies travel from the northern United States and Canada to the mountain forests of central Mexico. Their bright orange wings make the sky seem alive with motion. What makes this journey remarkable is its length and accuracy. Monarchs travel thousands of kilometers, yet the butterflies that arrive in Mexico are not the same ones that left the north. The journey takes several generations to complete, with each new group continuing the route their ancestors started. Scientists have been fascinated by how monarchs know where to go. Studies suggest they use the position of the sun as a kind of compass. They also appear to rely on an internal clock that adjusts for the sun’s movement during the day. Some experiments show that when the butterflies’ antennae are covered, they lose their sense of direction, suggesting that light sensors there play an important role. Monarchs also respond to temperature and wind, gliding on warm air currents to conserve energy during long flights. Despite their endurance, monarch populations have declined sharply in recent years. The biggest threats are habitat loss and the disappearance of milkweed plants, which are the only food source for monarch caterpillars. Conservation groups now encourage people to plant milkweed and create resting spots along the migration route. These efforts highlight how fragile and connected natural systems can be, even when they depend on something as small as a butterfly.

exercises.prompt: What is the main topic of the talk?

options.text: How bioluminescence affects ecosystems in the ocean depths
How deep-sea organisms use bioluminescence to survive
How scientists discovered bioluminescence in shallow waters
How light pollution interferes with the bioluminescence of marine animals

exercises.explanation: The talk focuses on how deep-sea organisms use bioluminescence to survive, communicate, and interact. Option A is too general, while C and D refer to unrelated ideas like shallow-water discoveries and light pollution. The main purpose is clearly tied to survival and communication beneath the ocean’s surface.
exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in a marine biology class. In the dark depths of the ocean, where sunlight never reaches, many organisms have developed the ability to produce their own light. This natural glow, known as bioluminescence, serves a variety of purposes. Some species use it to attract prey, while others rely on it to hide from predators. But one of the most intriguing uses is communication. For many deep-sea creatures, light is their language. Certain squid, for example, flash rhythmic pulses of blue light from their bodies to signal to potential mates or to coordinate movement within a group. In one species, these light displays become more complex during mating season, almost like a visual conversation. Other animals, such as the lanternfish, have glowing spots arranged along their sides that may help them recognize members of their own species in the darkness. Each pattern acts like an identification badge in a place where vision is limited. Researchers studying these organisms have discovered that light production is not always controlled by the animal alone. In some cases, bacteria living inside the creature’s body produce the glow. This cooperation between host and microbe shows how even in extreme environments, life depends on partnerships. Next, let’s look at how these biological light systems might inspire new forms of communication technology, such as underwater signaling devices or low-energy lighting systems.

exercises.title: Listening · Mcq 32
exercises.prompt: What is the main focus of the talk?

options.text: How early farmers domesticated animals to grow crops and build communities

How early communities in the Fertile Crescent developed agriculture

exercises.explanation: The talk explains how early communities in the Fertile Crescent began farming and developed stable settlements. The other options either focus on animals, empires, or climate, none of which represent the central theme. The passage highlights agriculture’s birth, not political or environmental crises.
exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in a history class. Around ten thousand years ago, in a region of the Middle East once known as the Fertile Crescent, a group of people began an experiment that would change human history. They were not building cities or empires yet. They were simply trying to survive in a landscape of grasslands and rivers that flooded each spring. Archaeological evidence from sites near the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers shows that small communities began gathering wild grains that grew after the floods. Over time, they noticed that seeds dropped near their camps sprouted again the next season. This observation marked the beginning of agriculture. One of the best-studied settlements from this period is Jericho, located near the Jordan River. The people there constructed circular houses from mud and built stone walls to protect their crops from animals and seasonal floods. Storage pits found beneath the floors suggest that they were saving food from one harvest to the next. This ability to store grain gave them security through harsh seasons and allowed the population to grow. Families no longer needed to move constantly in search of food, and social roles began to change as some members specialized in toolmaking and food preparation. These early farmers could not have known the long-term consequences of their innovation, yet their decision to plant and protect grain set in motion the rise of complex societies. In the next section, we will look at how similar communities laid the groundwork for the first civilizations.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 1-1
exercises.prompt: Thanks for joining me today. To begin, what kind of activities do you usually do to stay healthy? For instance, do you exercise regularly, focus on nutrition, or do something else?
exercises.sampleAnswer: I try to stay healthy mainly by running three times a week. There’s a big park near my dorm, and I like to go early in the morning before my first class. It helps me clear my head and gives me energy for the rest of the day. Besides exercise, I also cook most of my meals at home. I make simple dishes like rice, beans, and grilled chicken. I try to avoid fast food during the week, even though I have intense cravings for a cheeseburger once in a while. I usually prepare my lunches for the week on Sunday, that way, I don’t have to spend too much time cooking my meals every day. I wouldn’t say I follow a strict diet, but I do pay attention to what I eat.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 1-2
exercises.prompt: I see. When life gets stressful, do you prefer to deal with it by being physically active, like going for a walk or working out? Or would you rather quietly relax while reading a book or listening to music? Please explain.
exercises.sampleAnswer: When I’m stressed, I usually prefer to move around instead of sitting still. For example, during exam week last semester, at São Paulo University, I was so stressed that I couldn’t even focus on my notes. So every evening, I’d walk a loop around this huge park near my dorm. I remember one night, I just kept walking and breathing, and I could literally feel the tension leave my body. I was still stressed, but I felt much better. If I had tried to just read a book in my room, nothing would have changed. For me, my mind changes when something changes physically, which is why I have to move around when I need to change my mood.

exercises.sampleAnswer: Hmm, that’s an interesting question. I haven’t really thought about it much before, but yeah, I do think more people will depend on sleep medication in the future. Life just feels busier and noisier than it used to. People stay up late working or scrolling on their phones, and it messes with their sleep schedule. My older brother, for example, works at a hospital in São Paulo, and because of his night shifts, he started taking pills to fall asleep during the day. At first, it worked great, but now he says he can’t sleep without it. So I think that’s what’s going to happen to more people in the future.

For example, it’s much easier to eat healthy or exercise regularly if your city has good options, like safe parks, bike lanes, or grocery stores that sell fresh food. When I studied in Kyoto for a semester, I walked everywhere and ate balanced meals without even trying, because the environment supported it. But back home in Brazil, traffic is crazy and healthy food can be expensive, so people often grab fast food instead. So yes, personal choices matter, but society has to make those healthy choices possible in the first place.

exercises.prompt: The word “indicator” in the passage is closest in meaning to
exercises.passage:
Arctic Sea Ice and Global Climate

Arctic sea ice forms when ocean water freezes during winter and partially melts each summer. Over the past few decades, satellite observations have revealed a consistent decline in both the area and thickness of this ice. Scientists consider these measurements an important indicator of global climate change.

When sea ice melts, the darker ocean surface beneath it absorbs more sunlight, leading to additional warming—a process known as the ice-albedo feedback. This effect not only accelerates melting but also influences weather patterns far beyond the Arctic. Researchers have linked declining ice cover to shifts in jet streams and more extreme weather in temperate regions.

Melting sea ice also affects marine life. Species such as polar bears and seals depend on stable ice platforms for hunting and breeding. As these platforms disappear, animals must travel farther to find food, and survival rates drop. Indigenous communities that rely on sea ice for travel and hunting face similar challenges as their traditional routes become unsafe.

Scientists are monitoring seasonal cycles to understand how long-term warming might alter global ocean currents. Small changes in these currents can disrupt ecosystems and even affect rainfall patterns worldwide.

options.text: reaction
barrier
replacement
sign

exercises.explanation: D is correct because “indicator” means sign or signal. The passage says, “Scientists consider these measurements an important indicator of global climate change,” meaning the data are a sign of change. A, B, and C do not fit the context—“reaction,” “barrier,” and “replacement” are unrelated to evidence or signs.

exercises.title: Reading · Mcq 31
exercises.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
exercises.passage:
The Expansion of the Printing Press

When Johannes Gutenberg introduced movable-type printing in the mid-1400s, few realized how dramatically it would reshape Europe. His invention made it possible to reproduce texts faster and at a fraction of the cost of hand-copied manuscripts. Within decades, presses appeared in dozens of cities, turning what had once been rare into something nearly commonplace.

Early printers produced religious works such as Bibles and prayer books, but soon moved on to scientific and literary texts. The spread of printed material accelerated the exchange of ideas, allowing scholars to challenge accepted beliefs. This new accessibility to knowledge fueled movements like the Renaissance and the Reformation.

Not everyone welcomed the change. Religious and political authorities worried that printing could spread dissenting views. As a result, governments introduced censorship laws, sometimes banning specific books or requiring printers to obtain official licenses. Despite these restrictions, presses continued to multiply, and literacy rates rose steadily. By the seventeenth century, printing had become central to education and public debate. The technology not only preserved information but also democratized it, laying the foundation for modern journalism and mass communication.

options.text: Gutenberg’s invention transformed how information spread in Europe.
Printing presses replaced handwritten manuscripts overnight.
Governments supported the expansion of printing.
Religious works were the only materials produced by early printers.

exercises.explanation: A is correct because the passage emphasizes how Gutenberg’s invention transformed the spread of information across Europe. The first paragraph introduces printing as a technology that “reshaped Europe” by making books cheaper and faster to produce, while later paragraphs describe its influence on religion, science, and public debate. B is incorrect because the passage does not suggest handwritten manuscripts disappeared “overnight.” C is incorrect because governments often restricted printing through censorship, not fully supported it. D is incorrect because although early printers began with religious works, they soon expanded to scientific and literary texts.

exercises.title: Listening · Mcq 27
exercises.prompt: What is the main focus of the talk?

options.text: How modern agriculture has changed plant and animal evolution in dry climates

How desert plants survive extreme conditions through adaptations

exercises.explanation: The lecture focuses on how desert plants survive despite extreme heat and limited water, explaining their structural and behavioral adaptations, such as water storage and dormancy. This makes D the best answer. Option A focuses on agriculture, which is never mentioned. Option B centers on animals rather than plants. Option C explains desert formation, not adaptation.
exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in a biology class. Surviving in a desert requires remarkable strategies. In places where rainfall is rare and temperatures soar, plants have evolved specialized features that allow them to store water, reduce evaporation, and endure long periods of drought. One of the most familiar examples is the cactus. Its thick, fleshy stem acts as a reservoir, storing water collected during brief rains. The leaves have evolved into spines that protect the plant from animals while also reducing surface area, which limits water loss. Another adaptation is timing. Many desert plants remain dormant for months, waiting for a short burst of rain before sprouting leaves and flowers. Seeds may lie buried for years until just the right conditions trigger germination. Some plants, like the creosote bush, release chemicals into the soil that prevent other plants from growing too close, conserving limited moisture for themselves. These strategies reveal how even in extreme environments, life finds a way to balance scarcity and growth. Scientists studying desert ecosystems have discovered that these plants also influence local climates by stabilizing soil and reducing erosion. Their survival strategies inspire engineers developing materials and technologies designed to conserve water in dry regions. In the next part of this lecture, we’ll explore how similar adaptations appear in desert animals and what they reveal about the limits of life on Earth.

exercises.prompt: According to the talk, what did the student experiment reveal about memory?

options.text: Students who napped briefly learned more than those who slept fully.

exercises.explanation: The student experiment showed that those who slept after studying remembered significantly more than those who stayed awake. Sleep helped consolidate what they learned into long-term memory. Option A is wrong because the study didn’t focus on naps. Option B contradicts the results, and option C invents a group that studied in the morning, which wasn’t part of the design.
exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in a physiology class. Sleep is one of the body’s most vital yet mysterious processes. For centuries, it was thought to be a period of complete rest, but modern research shows that the brain remains surprisingly active. During sleep, it processes memories, restores energy, and performs maintenance that waking life does not allow. A series of studies with students has helped scientists understand this function more clearly. In one experiment, two groups were asked to learn a set of word pairs. One group studied in the evening and slept afterward, while the other stayed awake overnight. The next day, the group that had slept remembered far more. Brain scans showed that during deep sleep, areas involved in memory replayed patterns of activity seen during learning. This replay strengthened the connections between nerve cells, effectively transferring short-term information into long-term storage. Researchers have observed similar effects in animals. When rats navigate a maze and then fall asleep, their brains repeat the same electrical patterns seen during exploration, as if practicing the route. These findings suggest that sleep acts as a kind of rehearsal, turning daily experience into lasting knowledge. Despite its importance, sleep remains fragile in modern life. Bright screens, irregular schedules, and stress all interfere with its natural rhythm. Next, we’ll discuss how scientists are using brain imaging to study what happens in the mind during each stage of sleep and how this research could help treat sleep disorders.

options.text: The effect of air pollution on public health

exercises.explanation: The lecture explains why cities are hotter than rural areas and what consequences result from that difference, such as higher energy use and smog. It also describes efforts to cool cities. All of that fits D perfectly. Option A focuses only on pollution, Option B narrows the topic to design, and Option C lists solutions rather than summarizing the entire idea.
exercises.reference: Listen to a talk in an ecology class. In large metropolitan areas, temperatures often rise several degrees higher than in nearby rural regions. This pattern, known as the urban heat island effect, occurs when natural landscapes are replaced with surfaces that trap and store heat. Pavement, brick, and glass absorb sunlight throughout the day and release it slowly at night, preventing cities from cooling. Fewer trees and open spaces mean less shade and less evaporation, both of which normally keep temperatures down. The consequences extend beyond simple discomfort. In hotter cities, residents consume more electricity for cooling, increasing greenhouse gas emissions. Air pollutants also react more quickly in warm air, worsening smog and respiratory problems. Urban planners have begun to address these problems by experimenting with reflective roofing materials and a new kind of park called a “pocket park,” which lower neighborhood temperatures. In Los Angeles, for instance, a city program tested light colored road coatings and recorded surface temperatures several degrees lower than surrounding streets. Such efforts demonstrate how small design choices can influence the broader urban climate. Researchers studying these initiatives are now asking which combinations of vegetation, building materials, and public policies can produce the most sustainable results in rapidly growing cities.

exercises.explanation: Pavement and brick store heat during the day and release it slowly at night, keeping cities warm after sunset. That’s the key mechanism behind the “urban heat island” effect. Option A adds details about trapped heat that weren’t mentioned. Option C describes air movement but not heat storage. Option D incorrectly claims those surfaces reflect light when the problem is that they absorb it.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 1-1
exercises.prompt: I appreciate you taking the time to talk with me. Have you ever studied abroad, or do you know someone who has? What kind of experience did they have?
exercises.sampleAnswer: Yeah, actually, one of my closest friends, Minji, studied in Canada last year. She went to the University of British Columbia for a semester, and she absolutely loved it. She said the classes were smaller, and professors encouraged students to share their opinions, which was different from what we’re used to in Korea. She also mentioned how friendly people were. Like, strangers would hold doors open or start small talk on the bus. It was much easier for her to meet new people and make friends than she had expected. It wasn’t always easy, though; she said the first month felt really lonely. But by the end, she didn’t want to come back because she’d made so many international friends and felt more independent.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 1-2
exercises.prompt: Thanks for sharing that. If you had the opportunity, would you prefer to study abroad for a full degree program that would take more than two years, or just a short-term exchange? Why?
exercises.sampleAnswer: If I had the choice, I’d probably go for a short-term exchange, maybe one year at most. I think that’s enough time to experience life in another country without feeling like I’m completely starting over. It is hard for me to imagine living in another country for years. A full degree abroad sounds exciting, but it’s also expensive and far from family. I’m really close to my parents, and honestly, I think I’d miss home too much after a while. My cousin studied in the U.S. for four years, and she said the homesickness hit her hard around the second year. I really can’t imagine being away from my friends, family, and culture for too long. So for me, a one-year exchange would be perfect.

exercises.title: Speaking · Interview 1-3
exercises.prompt: That’s interesting. Many students now take online courses from foreign universities instead of traveling overseas. Do you think virtual programs will replace in-person study abroad in the future? Why or why not?
exercises.sampleAnswer: Hmm, that’s an interesting question. Well, to be honest, I don’t think so—not completely, at least. Online courses are great for saving money and time, but they can’t really replace the real experience of living abroad. When you’re physically there, you have to speak the language every day, try new food, and deal with cultural surprises. That’s what actually changes you. During COVID, I took an online summer course from a U.S. university, and it was interesting, but it didn’t feel like I was part of the community. I never met my classmates, and the discussions were kind of quiet. So, virtual programs will grow, but I think people will still want that face-to-face, real-life experience.

offers flexibility and autonomy, allowing people to design their work schedules around their lives rather than vice versa. This flexibility can lead to increased job satisfaction and productivity as people work e  in environments where they feel most comfortable.

Why or why not?” Digital nomadism offers a unique advantage by providing freedom and flexibility that boost productivity. I have worked from different locations while traveling and noticed that choosing the right environment helps me focus better on my tasks. I learned to set clear work hours during a semester abroad, which made it easier to enjoy new experiences without losing concentration on my studies. exercises.title: Reading · Mcq m1-16
exercises.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
exercises.passage:
The Mirror Test

Very young children cannot recognize themselves in a mirror; they usually achieve this milestone around 18 months of age. The ability to recognize oneself in the mirror is considered to be a key component of self-awareness and consciousness for humans. But what about animals?

For many years, scientists have known that members of the great ape family could recognize themselves in mirrors. They measured this by the “mirror test,” which involved putting a colored mark on an ape’s body, and then showing the ape its reflection in a mirror. If the ape tried to remove the mark on its own body, the scientists knew that the ape was recognizing its reflection.

Apes are close relatives of humans, but in recent years, scientists have discovered that other animals also pass the “mirror test.” Elephants and dolphins have shown signs of self-recognition. These, like apes, are highly intelligent animals. But in a more recent experiment, a type of fish called the cleaner fish tried to scrape a mark off its body when it saw itself in the mirror. This suggests that even less intelligent animals may possess more self-awareness than previously suspected.

options.text: Stages of early childhood development
Research on animal cognition
Differences between apes, elephants, and dolphins
Recent experiments on fish

exercises.title: Reading · Mcq m2-16
exercises.prompt: Which of the following best states a main idea of the passage?
exercises.passage:
The Paradox of Choice

The paradox of choice, a concept popularized by psychologist Barry Schwartz, suggests that more options can lead to less satisfaction. While the freedom to choose is fundamental to consumer culture, an overabundance of choices—from groceries to electronics—can overwhelm individuals, causing anxiety and decision fatigue. This paradox implies that the vast array of possibilities available today might actually diminish consumer contentment, as the fear of making the wrong choice looms large.

Research supports this notion. In an experiment, psychologist Sheena Iyengar found that shoppers were more likely to purchase jam when offered 6 varieties instead of 24. The limited selection eased the decision process, reducing the pressure to find the ‘perfect’ option and making the experience more enjoyable. This phenomenon reveals that fewer choices can sometimes make consumers happier, which is a valuable insight for marketers and retailers aiming to boost satisfaction by curating their offerings.

The paradox also has broader implications. In individualistic cultures, where personal choice is highly valued, the burden of decision-making can be significant. Conversely, collectivist cultures, which often provide fewer choices, report higher levels of contentment. This dynamic suggests that understanding cultural differences in consumer psychology can help businesses optimize their product strategies and enhance overall well-being.

options.text: Effective marketing strategies focus on increasing product options.
Modern consumer culture is driven by a demand for fewer products.
Individualism enhances consumer contentment.
Limiting consumer choices can lead to higher satisfaction.

exercises.passage:
The Paradox of Choice

The paradox of choice, a concept popularized by psychologist Barry Schwartz, suggests that more options can lead to less satisfaction. While the freedom to choose is fundamental to consumer culture, an overabundance of choices—from groceries to electronics—can overwhelm individuals, causing anxiety and decision fatigue. This paradox implies that the vast array of possibilities available today might actually diminish consumer contentment, as the fear of making the wrong choice looms large.

Research supports this notion. In an experiment, psychologist Sheena Iyengar found that shoppers were more likely to purchase jam when offered 6 varieties instead of 24. The limited selection eased the decision process, reducing the pressure to find the ‘perfect’ option and making the experience more enjoyable. This phenomenon reveals that fewer choices can sometimes make consumers happier, which is a valuable insight for marketers and retailers aiming to boost satisfaction by curating their offerings.

The paradox also has broader implications. In individualistic cultures, where personal choice is highly valued, the burden of decision-making can be significant. Conversely, collectivist cultures, which often provide fewer choices, report higher levels of contentment. This dynamic suggests that understanding cultural differences in consumer psychology can help businesses optimize their product strategies and enhance overall well-being.

Write for an Academic Discussion

Volunteerism refers to the act of offering your time and service without financial compensation to benefit
a community, organization, or cause. While many people volunteer mainly to help others, some
institutions have mandatory volunteer programs. High schools are one example, where students may be
required to complete a certain number of volunteer hours to graduate. What do you think? Should high
school students be required to do volunteer work? Why or why not?
Yes, I think high schools should require volunteer hours because it helps students
build a sense of civic responsibility. Many teenagers don’t naturally think about
helping others, and this requirement can introduce them to the idea that their time
and effort can make a real difference in the lives of others.
I don't think volunteer hours should be required because many students already
have limited free time. Some have part-time jobs or take care of younger siblings
’                     after school. Adding a mandatory volunteer requirement could create extra stress
and make it harder for those students to balance their existing responsibilities.
